title: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer
author: Mark Twain

chapters.title: Chapter 1. Look Behind You, Aunt!
chapters.text:
“Tom!”

No answer.

“Tom!”

No answer.

“Where has that boy gone, I wonder? You TOM!”

Aunt Polly pulled her glasses down and looked over them around the room. Then she pushed them up and looked under them. She almost never looked through them. They were for style, not for seeing.

She pushed a broom under the bed and found nothing but the cat. Then she heard a small noise behind her. She turned just in time to catch a boy by his jacket as he came out of the cupboard.

“There! What were you doing in there?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing! Look at your mouth. It's jam, that's what it is. I've told you forty times to leave that jam alone. Give me that stick.”

The stick went up into the air. Tom's eyes went wide.

“My! Look behind you, Aunt!”

The old lady turned quickly and lifted her skirts out of danger. The boy ran, climbed over the high wooden fence and was gone.

Aunt Polly stood there in surprise. Then she began to laugh softly.

“That boy! Will I never learn? He's played that trick on me a hundred times. But he never plays the same trick two days in a row, so how can anybody know what's coming?” She shook her head. “He's my dead sister's boy, poor thing, and I haven't got the heart to beat him. When I let him go, I feel I'm doing wrong. When I hit him, my old heart almost breaks.”

That afternoon Tom didn't go to school. He went swimming instead.

At supper Aunt Polly asked him some clever questions, hoping to catch him.

“It was very hot at school today, wasn't it, Tom?”

“Yes, ma'am.”

“Didn't you want to go swimming?”

Tom studied her face, but it told him nothing. “No, ma'am. Well, not very much.”

The old lady put out her hand and touched his shirt. It was dry, and she was disappointed. But Tom guessed what she was going to do next.

“Some of us put our heads under the pump,” he said quickly. “My hair's still damp. See?”

Aunt Polly was annoyed. Then she had a new idea.

“Tom, this morning I sewed your shirt collar shut with white thread, so you couldn't take your shirt off. Show me.”

Tom opened his jacket. The collar was still sewn tightly.

“Well! Go along with you, then. I was sure you'd been swimming. But I forgive you, Tom.”

Then Tom's half-brother Sid spoke. Sid was a quiet boy. He never did anything wrong, and he never let anybody forget it.

“Didn't you sew his collar with white thread, Aunt? Now it's black.”

“Why, I did sew it with white! Tom!”

But Tom was already at the door. “Siddy, I'll beat you for that,” he said, and he ran.

Outside, his bad mood soon disappeared. He was walking down the street, practising a new way of whistling, when he saw a stranger: a boy a little bigger than himself. New boys were rare in the little town of St. Petersburg. And this one was wearing shoes, a tie and a smart hat on a weekday!

Tom hated him at once.

The two boys walked around each other in a slow circle, staring.

“I can beat you!” said Tom.

“I'd like to see you try.”

“Well, I can do it.”

“No, you can't.”

“Yes, I can.”

“No, you can't.”

There was an uncomfortable pause. Then Tom drew a line in the dust with his toe. “I dare you to step over that.”

The new boy stepped over it at once.

A second later they were rolling in the dirt like two cats, pulling hair and tearing clothes. Soon Tom was sitting on top of the stranger and hitting him with his fists.

“Say 'enough'!”

At last the boy said it and went away, crying and covered in dust.

Tom got home late that night and climbed in through his window. But his aunt was waiting for him. When she saw the state of his clothes, her face became hard.

Tom's free Saturday was going to become a day of hard work.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Wonderful Fence
chapters.text:
Saturday morning came, and the whole summer world was bright and fresh.

Tom came out into the street with a bucket of whitewash, a kind of cheap white paint, and a long brush. He looked at the fence, and all the joy left him. It was thirty yards long and nine feet high. Life suddenly seemed empty.

He painted one narrow white line along the top board, compared it with the huge grey fence and sat down, miserable. Soon the other boys would come along and laugh at him. The thought burned like fire.

Then an idea came to him. A great, beautiful idea.

He calmly went back to work. Ben Rogers, the boy whose laughter Tom feared most of all, was coming down the street. Ben was eating an apple and pretending to be a steamboat on the Mississippi.

“Ding-dong-dong! Stop her, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling!” He turned slowly in the road, making big circles with his arms like paddle wheels. “Ch-ch-ch-chow!”

Tom paid no attention to the steamboat.

“Hi! You're in trouble, aren't you? You have to work!”

No answer. Tom looked at his last line with the eye of an artist. Ben came closer. Tom's mouth watered for the apple, but he didn't stop.

Then he turned round, as if in surprise. “Why, it's you, Ben! I didn't notice.”

“Say, I'm going swimming. But of course you'd rather work, wouldn't you?”

Tom looked at him. “What do you call work?”

“Why, isn't that work?”

Tom answered carelessly, “Well, maybe it is, and maybe it isn't. All I know is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”

“Oh, come on. You don't mean that you like it?”

The brush kept moving. “Like it? Well, I don't see why I shouldn't like it. Does a boy get a chance to paint a fence every day?”

That put things in a new light. Ben stopped eating his apple. Tom moved his brush gently, stepped back to admire the effect and added a touch here and there. Ben watched every move.

“Say, Tom, let me paint a little.”

“No, no. I'm sorry, Ben. Aunt Polly is very particular about this fence. It has to be done very carefully. I don't think there's one boy in a thousand, maybe two thousand, who can do it the right way.”

“Oh, please. Just let me try. I'll give you the core of my apple.”

“Well, here... No, Ben, I'm afraid...”

“I'll give you all of it!”

Tom handed over the brush with sadness on his face but joy in his heart. And while the steamboat worked and sweated in the sun, the retired artist sat in the shade, ate the apple, and planned how to catch more fools.

There were plenty of them. They came to laugh, but they stayed to paint. When Ben was tired, Billy Fisher bought the next turn for a kite. Johnny Miller paid with a dead rat on a string. And so it went on, hour after hour.

By the middle of the afternoon Tom was rich. He had twelve marbles, a piece of blue glass, a key that couldn't open anything, a kitten with only one eye, a brass doorknob, a dog collar but no dog, and four pieces of orange peel. And the fence had three coats of whitewash on it. The whitewash ran out just in time to save the other boys from losing everything they owned.

Without knowing it, Tom had discovered a great law of human life: if you want people to want something, just make it hard to get.

Tom went inside to find his aunt. “May I go and play now, Aunt?” he asked. “It's all done.”

“Tom, don't lie to me. I can't bear it.”

She went out to look. When she saw the fence, painted and painted again, she could hardly speak.

“Well, I never! You can work when you want to, Tom.” She gave him an apple and a little speech about the value of hard work. While she was speaking, Tom stole a cake.

Then he walked out into the bright afternoon, a rich and happy boy. He had no idea that in a few minutes his heart was going to be stolen.

chapters.title: Chapter 3. Becky Thatcher
chapters.text:
Tom was passing Judge Thatcher's house when he saw a girl in the garden. She was new in town: a lovely little thing with blue eyes, yellow hair in two long plaits and a white summer dress.

A minute earlier, Tom had been in love with Amy Lawrence. Now Amy was gone from his heart, like a visitor who had left without saying goodbye.

He began to show off. He stood on his hands and walked along the top of the fence, all without looking at the girl once. Well, almost. When he did look, she was walking towards the house. Tom's heart sank. But at the door she stopped, and she threw a flower over the fence.

Tom picked it up and put it inside his jacket, next to his heart.

On Monday morning, on his way to school, he met Huckleberry Finn. Huck was the son of the town drunk. He never went to school or to church. He slept in doorways in good weather and in empty barrels in bad weather. He wore a grown man's old clothes and smoked a pipe. All the mothers in town hated him. All the boys wished they were him.

Huck was carrying a dead cat.

“Hello, Huckleberry! What's that for?”

“For curing warts.” He held up a hand covered in small, hard lumps.

“How?”

“You take your cat to the graveyard at midnight, where somebody wicked is buried. When the devils come for him, you throw the cat after them and say, 'Devil follow body, cat follow devil, warts follow cat, I'm done with you!' That'll get rid of any wart.”

“When are you going?”

“Tonight. I reckon the devils will come for old Hoss Williams. They buried him on Saturday.”

“Can I come with you?”

“Sure, if you ain't scared.”

“Scared! Not me. Meow under my window.”

Tom arrived at school very late. The teacher, Mr. Dobbins, was sitting in his big chair.

“Thomas Sawyer! Why are you late again?”

Tom was ready with a lie. But then he saw two long yellow plaits, and an empty seat beside them on the girls' side of the room.

“I stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn!”

The whole class went silent.

“You... you did what?”

“Stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn.”

Mr. Dobbins beat him until his arm was tired. Then he said, “Now, sir, go and sit with the girls! And let this be a warning to you.”

That was exactly what Tom wanted. He sat down next to the girl with the yellow hair, and he soon learned her name: Becky Thatcher. He drew a house on his slate for her. Then he wrote something and covered it with his hand. Becky begged to see it. At last he moved his hand away. There were three words: I love you.

“Oh, you bad thing!” Becky hit his hand, but her face went pink, and she looked pleased.

At lunchtime, when the schoolroom was empty, Tom asked her if she would like to be engaged: to promise to marry him one day.

“It's easy. You just tell a boy you'll never have anybody but him, ever, ever, ever. And then you kiss. That's all.”

After a lot of shy refusals, she whispered “I love you” in his ear and let him kiss her.

“Now it's all done, Becky. And after this you must never love anybody but me, and never marry anybody but me. And we'll always walk to school together, because that's what you do when you're engaged. Me and Amy Lawrence always...”

He stopped. It was too late. Becky's big eyes filled with tears.

“Oh, Tom! Then I'm not the first!”

She pushed his arm away. He offered her his greatest treasure, the brass doorknob. She knocked it to the floor.

So Tom walked out of the school and away into the woods. He lay under a tree all afternoon and thought how nice it would be to die, just for a little while, so that Becky would be sorry.

But by evening he had something better to think about. At midnight Huck Finn was going to meow under his window.

chapters.title: Chapter 4. Midnight in the Graveyard
chapters.text:
At half past nine Tom and Sid were sent to bed. Tom lay awake in the dark and listened to the clock strike ten, then eleven. At last he heard it: “Meow!”

A minute later he was out of the window and across the shed roof. Huck was waiting with his dead cat.

The graveyard was on a hill outside the village. The names on its old graves had worn away long ago. A soft wind moaned in the trees. To Tom it sounded like the voices of the dead, complaining that somebody had disturbed them.

The boys found the new grave of Hoss Williams and hid behind three big trees a few feet away. The silence was terrible.

“Hucky,” Tom whispered at last, “do you think the dead people like us being here?”

“I wish I knew. It's awful quiet, ain't it?”

Suddenly Huck caught his arm. “Sh! What's that?”

There were voices. A light was moving through the darkness towards them.

“It's the devils!” Huck whispered. “Three of them! Can you pray, Tom?”

Tom began to pray, but Huck stopped him. “They're people! That's old Muff Potter's voice. He's drunk, as usual.”

“And that other voice is Injun Joe's,” whispered Tom.

“Oh, him. I'd rather they were devils.”

The third man was young Dr. Robinson. Potter and Injun Joe were pushing a wheelbarrow with two spades in it, and at the new grave they began to dig. The doctor wanted a body to study, and he was paying these men to steal one.

At last they lifted out the coffin and tied the body onto the wheelbarrow.

“Now it's ready, Doctor,” said Potter. “Give us another five dollars, or here it stays.”

“What do you mean?” said the doctor. “You wanted your money in advance, and I've paid you.”

“Yes, and you've done more than that,” said Injun Joe, coming closer. “Five years ago I came to your father's kitchen to ask for something to eat, and you sent me away. I said I'd get even with you if it took a hundred years. Then your father put me in jail. Now I've got you, and you're going to pay!”

He shook his fist in the doctor's face. Suddenly the doctor hit him and knocked him to the ground. Potter dropped his knife.

“Don't you hit my partner!” he shouted, and the next moment he and the doctor were fighting in the grass.

Injun Joe jumped up with burning eyes. He picked up Potter's knife and moved around the two men like a cat, waiting for his chance.

The doctor pulled himself free, grabbed the heavy wooden board with Hoss Williams's name on it and knocked Potter to the ground with it. At that same moment Injun Joe drove the knife into the young man's chest.

The doctor fell on top of Potter. Just then a cloud covered the moon, and the two terrified boys ran off into the dark.

When the moon came out again, Injun Joe was standing over the two men. The doctor whispered something, took one long breath and was still.

“That score is settled,” said Injun Joe quietly.

He took the money from the doctor's pockets. Then he put the knife into Potter's open hand and sat down to wait. At last Potter began to move. He looked at the knife in his hand, then at the doctor, and he dropped the knife with a shiver.

“Lord, Joe, what happened?”

“It's a dirty business,” Joe said calmly. “Why did you do it? You two were fighting. He hit you with the board, and you fell. Then you got up, half crazy, grabbed the knife and put it in him.”

Potter went white. “I was drunk. I can't remember a thing. Oh, Joe, I never meant to do it! Don't tell anybody!”

“You've always been fair with me, Muff Potter, and I won't tell on you.”

Potter thanked him, crying, and ran away into the night. He forgot his knife.

Injun Joe looked down at it and smiled. Then he too disappeared, and the dead man, the empty coffin and the open grave were left alone under the moon.

chapters.title: Chapter 5. A Terrible Secret
chapters.text:
The boys ran all the way back towards the village, too frightened to speak. Every tree looked like a man. At last they ran through the open door of the old tannery, an empty building where people used to make leather, and fell down in the dark.

“Huckleberry,” Tom whispered, when he could breathe again, “what's going to happen?”

“If Doctor Robinson dies, somebody will hang for it.”

“Who's going to tell? Us?”

“Are you crazy? If we tell, and Injun Joe doesn't hang, he'll kill us. As sure as we're lying here.”

So they agreed to keep the secret. But a promise didn't seem enough for something so terrible. Tom found a clean piece of wood, and with a piece of red stone he wrote slowly:

Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer swear they will keep quiet about This and they wish they may drop down dead if they ever tell, and rot.

Then each of them pricked his thumb with a pin and signed his name in blood. They buried the wood next to the wall.

Just then a dog began to howl outside, a long, sad cry in the night. Everybody knew what that meant: if a stray dog howled at you at night, you were going to die soon.

“Oh, Tom, it's us! It's howling at us!”

Shaking, Tom looked through a crack in the wall. Then he whispered, “No, Huck. Its back is to us.”

They looked out together. A few feet from the dog, in the shadow of the wall, a man was lying asleep and snoring. The dog was pointing its nose straight at him. It was Muff Potter.

Tom got home just before dawn. But Sid had been awake, and in the morning Aunt Polly knew everything. Nobody beat him. Instead, Aunt Polly cried and asked him why he wanted to break her old heart. That was a thousand times worse.

At school he was punished for missing lessons the afternoon before. When he got back to his desk, he found something wrapped in paper. He opened it, and his heart broke. It was his brass doorknob. Becky had given it back.

At noon the terrible news reached the village: the young doctor had been murdered in the graveyard, and Muff Potter's knife had been found next to the body. Everybody hurried up the hill to see. Tom went too, and he found Huck there in the crowd.

Then the sheriff brought Muff Potter. The poor man's face was grey with fear. When he saw the dead doctor, he began to cry.

“I didn't do it, friends,” he said. “On my word, I never did it.”

“Is this your knife?” the sheriff asked.

Potter fell to his knees. “Tell them, Joe. Tell them. It's no use any more.”

And Injun Joe told his story, calmly and clearly, without one honest word in it. The two boys stood there and waited for God to send lightning down on his head. Nothing happened. Injun Joe went on talking, and the sky stayed blue. From that moment he was the most frightening man in the world to them.

For a week afterwards Tom slept badly. One morning Sid said, “You talk in your sleep, Tom. Last night you kept saying, 'It's blood! It's blood!' And you said, 'Don't make me tell!' Tell what?”

Tom went pale, but Aunt Polly came to his rescue. “It's that awful murder. I dream about it every night myself.”

After that, Tom tied a cloth around his jaw every night so that he couldn't talk. He said it was toothache.

The little jail stood at the edge of the village, and it had a small window with iron bars. Almost every day Tom and Huck crept up to it and passed small presents through it to Muff Potter: some tobacco, a few matches, a piece of cake.

“You've been mighty good to me, boys,” Potter said one evening, holding the bars. “Better than anybody else in this town. I won't forget it.”

Every kind word hurt Tom like a knife. Only two people in St. Petersburg could save Muff Potter, and both of them were too frightened to say a single word.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. Pirates on the Island
chapters.text:
Soon after that, Becky stopped coming to school. She was ill, people said. Tom stopped caring about anything.

Aunt Polly was worried. She believed in every new medicine she read about, and she tried them all on Tom. Nothing helped. At last she bought a bottle of Pain-killer. It tasted like liquid fire, and she gave him a spoonful every day.

One morning Peter, the cat, came up to Tom and looked hungrily at the spoon.

“Don't ask for it unless you really want it, Peter,” said Tom. Peter showed that he really wanted it, so Tom opened the cat's mouth and poured the Pain-killer in.

Peter jumped six feet into the air. He gave a terrible cry and ran round and round the room, knocking over flower pots and crashing into furniture. Then he flew out of the open window. Aunt Polly stood watching, amazed.

“Tom, what's the matter with that cat?”

“I don't know, Aunt,” said Tom, laughing too hard to breathe. “Cats always act like that when they're having a good time.”

Then she saw the spoon. “Tom! Why did you do that to a poor dumb animal?”

“I did it because I felt sorry for him. He hasn't got any aunt.”

Aunt Polly stopped. If it was cruel for the cat, maybe it was cruel for the boy too. Her eyes grew soft. “I was trying to do my best for you, Tom,” she said gently. After that there was no more Pain-killer.

Soon Becky came back to school. Tom was so happy that he ran around the schoolyard, shouting, jumping over fences and standing on his head. But Becky turned her nose up.

“Some people think they're very smart,” she said to nobody in particular. “Always showing off!”

Tom's face burned. He walked away into the woods, and he made a dark decision. Nobody loved him. Very well. He would leave home for ever and become a pirate.

On the road he met his best friend, Joe Harper. Joe's mother had just whipped him for drinking some cream, and he had never even touched it. So he was ready to run away too. That afternoon they found Huck Finn, who was always ready for anything, and the three of them made a plan.

At midnight they met at the river with everything they could carry. Tom brought a ham, Joe brought some bacon, and Huck brought a frying pan and some tobacco. They took a small raft and floated quietly down the great Mississippi to Jackson's Island, three miles below the town. Nobody lived there. It was perfect.

Tom gave everybody a pirate's name. He was the Black Avenger of the Spanish Main. Joe was the Terror of the Seas. Huck was Huck the Red-Handed.

They made a fire in the forest, cooked bacon and ate like kings. No school, no church, no washing. This was the life!

The next morning they swam, fished and explored the island. In the afternoon, while they were lying in the shade, they heard a strange sound across the water.

Boom!

They ran to the edge of the trees. In the middle of the river was the town's ferryboat, crowded with people. Smoke came from the ferryboat's side, and then another dull boom rolled across the water.

“They're firing a cannon,” said Tom. “Somebody's drowned. When a person drowns, they fire a cannon over the water. It makes the body come up to the top.”

“I wonder who it is,” said Huck.

Suddenly Tom shouted, “Boys, I know who's drowned! It's us!”

They felt like heroes at once. The whole town was looking for them! People were crying for them! Being a pirate was even better than they had expected.

But when night came and the fire burned low, Joe and Huck grew quiet. Each of them was thinking about home.

Tom waited until they were both asleep. Then he took two pieces of white bark from a tree and wrote something on each. He left one beside Joe's hat and put the other in his pocket. Then he slipped away through the trees towards the river.

chapters.title: Chapter 7. At Their Own Funeral
chapters.text:
Tom swam to the far shore. There he hid in the little rowing boat behind the ferryboat and rode across to the town without anybody seeing him.

The lights were still on in Aunt Polly's house. Through the window he saw his aunt, Sid, his cousin Mary and Joe Harper's mother, all sitting together. Tom crept in through the door and hid under the bed.

“He wasn't bad,” Aunt Polly was saying, “only full of mischief. He never meant any harm, and he was the best-hearted boy that ever was.” And she began to cry.

“It was just the same with my Joe,” sobbed Mrs. Harper. “Only yesterday I whipped him for drinking that cream. And then I remembered that I'd thrown it out myself because it was sour! And now I'll never see him again!”

The town believed the boys had gone swimming and drowned. If they weren't found by Sunday, there would be a funeral for them at church.

Tom felt so sorry for his aunt that he wanted to jump out from under the bed and throw his arms around her. He had the piece of bark in his pocket. But then a better idea came to him, a wonderful, dramatic idea, and he stayed where he was.

When the house was quiet, he came out. Aunt Polly was asleep in her chair. He bent down and kissed her. Then he crept out again, borrowed a small boat and rowed back to the island. He arrived at breakfast time, just as Joe was saying, “Tom's true, Huck. He'll come back.”

“And here I am!” said Tom, and he walked out of the trees like a hero in a play.

That night a terrible storm hit the island and blew their tent away. The next day Joe and Huck were homesick and wanted to go home. So Tom told them his secret plan. They shouted with joy and agreed to stay.

On Sunday morning the church bell rang slowly and sadly. The whole town came, dressed in black. Becky Thatcher walked alone in the empty schoolyard, crying. “Oh, if I only had that brass doorknob again!” she thought. “Now I've got nothing to remember him by.”

In the church the minister spoke about the three boys for a long time. People who had always called the boys little monsters now remembered them as little angels. Soon the whole church was crying, and the minister was crying too.

Then there was a noise at the back of the church. Everybody turned round. And down the aisle came the three dead boys! Tom was first, Joe was next, and Huck came last, in his dirty old clothes, looking very embarrassed. They had been hiding in the gallery upstairs and listening to their own funeral.

Aunt Polly, Mary and the Harpers threw themselves on their boys and kissed them. Poor Huck stood alone, not knowing where to look.

“Aunt Polly, it's not fair,” said Tom. “Somebody's got to be glad to see Huck.”

“And so they shall. I'm glad to see him, poor motherless thing!” said Aunt Polly, and she kissed Huck too, which made him even more uncomfortable.

Then the minister shouted, “Praise God! Sing, and put your hearts into it!” And the whole town sang until the roof shook. Tom looked around at all the faces, and he decided it was the proudest moment of his life.

A few days later Aunt Polly found out that Tom had been home that night. She was deeply hurt.

“You let me cry for you, Tom, when you could have told me you were alive!”

“But I came to tell you, Aunt. Truly I did. I wrote it down for you.”

She didn't believe him. But later, when he had gone out, she took his old jacket from the cupboard and looked in the pocket. There she found a piece of bark, and on it, in Tom's handwriting, were the words: “We ain't dead. We are only off being pirates.”

Aunt Polly read it twice, and her eyes filled with tears.

“I could forgive that boy now,” she said, “if he'd done a million wrong things!”

chapters.title: Chapter 8. Tom Takes the Punishment
chapters.text:
Tom was a hero now. The smaller boys followed him everywhere, and the bigger ones wished they had been pirates too. But Becky still wouldn't speak to him, and that spoiled everything.

The teacher, Mr. Dobbins, had a secret. He kept a book locked in his desk, and every day, when the class was busy, he took it out and read it. Every boy and girl in the school wanted to know what it was.

One day at lunchtime Becky was passing the teacher's desk, and she saw that the key was in the lock. Nobody was around. She opened the desk, took out the book and began to turn the pages. It was a book about the human body, full of pictures. She was looking at one of them when a shadow fell across the page. Tom Sawyer had come in through the door.

Becky tried to close the book quickly, and she tore the picture right down the middle. She pushed the book back into the desk, then turned on Tom with tears of anger in her eyes.

“Tom Sawyer, you're just as mean as you can be, creeping up on a person like that! Now Mr. Dobbins will whip me, and I've never been whipped at school in my life!” And she ran out of the room.

Tom stood there, confused. “What a silly girl,” he thought. “A whipping is nothing!” But then he thought again. When the teacher found the torn page, he would ask every pupil who did it. And Becky would go red in the face, and everybody would know.

After lunch Mr. Dobbins sat down and opened his book. Tom watched Becky. She looked like a frightened rabbit. A moment later the teacher looked up, and every pupil looked down.

“Who tore this book?”

There was not a sound. You could hear a pin drop.

“Benjamin Rogers, did you tear this book?”

“No, sir.”

He went along the boys' benches, then turned to the girls.

“Amy Lawrence?”

“No, sir.”

“Gracie Miller?”

“No, sir.”

The next girl was Becky Thatcher. She was shaking from head to foot.

“Rebecca Thatcher, look at me. Did you tear this book?”

Suddenly an idea shot through Tom's head like lightning. He jumped to his feet and shouted, “I did it!”

The whole school stared at him. How could anybody be so foolish? Tom walked up to the front to take his punishment, and on the way he saw the look in Becky's eyes. It was full of surprise, gratitude and love, and it was worth a hundred whippings.

Mr. Dobbins gave him the hardest whipping that anybody could remember. Then he ordered Tom to stay at school for two hours after everybody else had gone home. Tom didn't mind at all. He knew who would be waiting for him outside.

That night he went to sleep with Becky's words in his ears: “Tom, how could you be so noble?”

Soon after that the summer holidays began. The days were long and hot, and the boys had all the time in the world. But a dark cloud hung over Tom. Muff Potter's trial was coming, and the whole town was talking about nothing else. Every time somebody mentioned the murder, Tom felt a cold shiver go down his back.

One day he took Huck to a quiet place. “Huck, have you ever told anybody about that night?”

“Of course not. You know I haven't. I don't want to be killed by Injun Joe.”

“Me neither. But Huck, poor old Muff Potter. He's been kind to us. He fixed my kite once, and he gave you fish when you were hungry.”

“I know,” said Huck sadly. “But they say he's going to hang.”

The two boys looked at each other in silence. Then they swore their oath again, even more seriously than before.

But on the evening before the trial, Tom stayed out very late. When he came home, he climbed in through the window, his face white and his eyes bright. He lay awake for hours. He had done something, and he couldn't take it back.

chapters.title: Chapter 9. The Trial
chapters.text:
The next morning the whole town crowded into the courtroom. Muff Potter was brought in with chains on his legs. He looked pale and thin, and he kept his eyes on the floor. Injun Joe sat a few rows away, as calm as ever.

The lawyers began. One witness said he had seen Potter washing himself in the river early on the morning after the murder. Another said that the knife next to the body was Potter's. A third told the court how Potter had cried and almost confessed when he was brought to the graveyard.

After each witness, Potter's lawyer said, “I have no questions.” People in the court looked at each other and whispered. Wasn't this man going to try to save his client? Was he going to let him hang without a fight?

Then Potter's lawyer stood up. “Your Honour, at the start of this trial we planned to prove that our client was drunk and didn't know what he was doing. We have changed our minds.” He turned to the clerk. “Call Thomas Sawyer!”

Everybody in the room turned to look as Tom walked to the front. He was very pale, and he looked badly frightened. He put his hand on the Bible and promised to tell the truth.

“Thomas Sawyer, where were you at midnight on the seventeenth of June?”

Tom looked at Injun Joe's iron face, and his voice disappeared. Then, slowly, it came back. “In the graveyard.”

“A little louder, please. Don't be afraid. Were you near the grave of Hoss Williams?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Were you hidden?”

“I was behind the big trees near the grave.”

Injun Joe moved slightly in his seat.

“Was anybody with you?”

“Yes, sir. But I don't want to say who...”

“Very well. We'll keep that for now. Tell us everything that happened, my boy. Tell it in your own way. Don't leave anything out, and don't be afraid.”

Tom began, slowly at first. But as he went on, the words came more and more easily. Soon there was no other sound in the room but his voice. Every eye was fixed on him. People held their breath as he told about the digging, the coffin, the argument about money and the fight in the moonlight.

“...and then the doctor picked up the board and hit Muff Potter, and Muff Potter fell down, and Injun Joe jumped forward with the knife, and...”

Crash! Quick as lightning, Injun Joe jumped up, pushed people out of his way and threw himself through the window. Glass flew everywhere. In a second he was gone.

Tom was a hero again, a much bigger hero than before. The old men of the town shook his hand. Some people even said he might be President one day, if he wasn't hanged first.

Muff Potter was set free, and the whole town was suddenly just as kind to him as it had been cruel before. People always do that. It isn't anything to be proud of, so it's probably better not to say any more about it.

Tom's days were full of glory. But his nights were full of terror. Injun Joe was in all his dreams, and he always had a knife in his hand.

Poor Huck was in the same state. Tom had told the lawyer the whole story the night before the trial, but he had kept Huck's name out of it. Even so, Huck was terribly afraid that his part would come out.

“Tom, a promise ain't worth anything any more,” he said sadly. “Not after this.”

The town offered a reward for Injun Joe. A detective came all the way from St. Louis. He looked around, shook his head and found what he called a clue. But you can't hang a clue for murder. After a while the detective went home, and Tom felt just as unsafe as before.

The days went slowly by, and each one took away a little of Tom's fear. Injun Joe was far away now, people said. He would never dare to come back.

People were wrong.

chapters.title: Chapter 10. The Haunted House
chapters.text:
There comes a time in every boy's life when he has a great desire to go somewhere and dig for buried treasure. That time came to Tom one summer morning, and he went straight to find Huck Finn.

“Where would we dig?” asked Huck, who was always ready for any adventure that was fun and didn't cost money.

“Oh, almost anywhere. Robbers always bury their treasure under a dead tree, or in an old haunted house.”

They dug under a dead tree on Cardiff Hill all afternoon and found nothing at all. So they decided to try the haunted house. It stood alone in an empty valley, and no one had lived there for years. People said ghosts walked there at night, so the boys agreed to go in the daytime. They didn't go on Friday, though. Everybody knew that Friday was an unlucky day.

On Saturday, at noon, they arrived with a pick and a shovel. The house was silent. The grass grew through the floor, the windows were broken, and spiders' webs hung everywhere. The boys spoke in whispers. They left their tools in a corner and went carefully up the old stairs to look around the top floor.

Suddenly Tom put his finger to his lips. “Sh! Listen!”

Somebody was coming. The boys lay down flat on the dusty floor and looked through a hole in the boards.

Two men came in. One was a ragged stranger. The other was an old Spaniard with long white hair, a big hat and green glasses. Everybody in town had seen him lately. He was deaf and dumb, people said; he couldn't hear or speak.

But now the Spaniard spoke.

“Is everything ready for the job?”

The boys nearly died of fright. They knew that voice. It was Injun Joe!

The two men talked about a “dangerous job” in town. Then they ate, drank some whisky and fell asleep. Upstairs, the boys hardly breathed. Hours seemed to pass.

At last the men woke up. They had a bag with six hundred dollars in it, money they had stolen, and they decided to hide it in the house. Injun Joe knelt down in a corner and began to dig with his knife. Suddenly the knife hit something hard.

“What's this?” he said. “It's a box!”

He dug faster. Then he lifted out a small wooden box and opened it. It was full of gold coins.

Upstairs, the boys almost shouted with joy. Real treasure! Thousands of dollars!

“It's Murrel's gang of robbers that buried this,” said the stranger. “They were here one summer, years ago.”

“And there's more money than we'll ever need,” said Injun Joe. Then he stopped. He had seen the boys' pick and shovel in the corner, with fresh earth on them. “Who brought these here? Somebody's been here! Do you think they're upstairs?”

He took out his knife and started up the stairs. The boys lay frozen with terror. One step, two steps... and then the rotten old wood gave way, and Injun Joe fell to the ground with a crash.

He stood up, swearing. “Well, if anybody's up there, they can stay there.”

“Where shall we take the box?” asked the stranger.

“Not here. Somebody might come back. We'll hide it in my den, my secret place. Number Two, under the cross. And then there's one more job I have to do before I leave this town.” His eyes burned. “Revenge!”

As night fell, the two men left, carrying the box between them. The boys came down slowly, weak with fear. They had been so close to the treasure! Why, oh why, had they left their tools downstairs?

“Number Two, under the cross,” Tom repeated. “What does it mean? Where is it?”

“I don't know,” said Huck. “But Tom, did you hear what he said about revenge?”

Tom felt cold all over.

“Revenge?” he whispered. “Huck... what if he means us?”

chapters.title: Chapter 11. Lost in the Cave
chapters.text:
For days Tom and Huck watched the town, looking for Injun Joe and the box of gold. Then Tom forgot everything. Becky's mother had agreed to a picnic, and Becky had invited all her friends.

On Saturday morning a big steamboat carried a crowd of happy children down the river. After lunch somebody shouted, “Who's ready for the cave?”

Everybody was. McDougal's cave was a huge maze of tunnels under the hill. People said you could walk in it for days and never reach the end. Nobody knew all of it.

The children took candles and ran inside, laughing and screaming. They played hide-and-seek in the dark passages until evening. Then the steamboat's bell rang, and everybody went home tired and happy. Becky was going to spend the night with her friend Susy Harper, and Tom said he would stay with Joe. Nobody counted the children on the boat.

That night Huck was keeping watch alone in the dark street when two men slipped past him. One of them was the Spaniard. Huck followed them up Cardiff Hill. They stopped in the bushes near the house of the Widow Douglas, a kind old lady who often gave Huck food.

“Her husband was a judge, and he was hard on me,” Injun Joe was whispering. “He had me whipped in front of the whole town like a horse. He's dead now, so she'll pay for it. I'll mark her face so she'll never forget me.”

Huck had never been so frightened in his life. But he crept away, then ran as fast as he could to the house of an old Welshman, Mr. Jones, and banged on his door.

“Let me in, quick! I'll tell everything!”

A few minutes later the Welshman and his two big sons were climbing the hill with guns. Huck didn't wait to see more. He heard shots and shouts, and he ran. The two men escaped in the dark, but the widow was safe. And Huck made the Welshman promise never to tell anybody who had warned him.

On Sunday morning, after church, Mrs. Thatcher came up to Aunt Polly.

“Is my Becky at your house? Mrs. Harper says she never came to them last night.”

Aunt Polly's face went white. “No. And Tom didn't come home either. I thought he was with Joe.”

Joe Harper hadn't seen Tom. Nobody had seen Becky. Then a boy remembered: he hadn't seen them on the steamboat. They must still be in the cave!

In a few minutes the whole town knew. Two hundred men rushed to McDougal's cave.

Deep inside the cave, Tom and Becky had wandered away from the others. They found beautiful passages with shining walls, and an underground lake, and they followed one passage after another. Then thousands of bats flew at their candles, and the children ran. When they stopped, they had no idea where they were.

“Tom, I can't hear the others any more.”

“I'll find the way, Becky. Don't worry.”

But every passage looked the same. They walked and walked. Tom shouted, and only his own voice came back to him, a long, ghostly echo. Becky began to cry.

They had one candle left. They sat down by a little spring of water, and Tom blew the candle out to save it. The darkness was complete. Time passed, and they didn't know if it was day or night. They shared their last piece of cake. They slept, woke up and slept again.

At last Tom had an idea. He had a kite string in his pocket. He tied one end to a rock, and he went down a side passage on his hands and knees, letting out the string behind him as he went.

A little further on, the passage turned a corner. Suddenly a light appeared from behind a rock: a human hand holding a candle! Tom gave a shout of joy.

Then the rest of the body came out from behind the rock.

It was Injun Joe.

chapters.title: Chapter 12. The Treasure
chapters.text:
Tom couldn't move. But to his amazement, Injun Joe turned and ran away into the dark. The echo had changed Tom's voice, and Joe hadn't recognised it.

Tom crawled back to Becky, shaking, but he said nothing about what he had seen. Becky was very weak now, and she wanted to give up. So Tom took his string and tried another passage, then another. At the end of the third one he saw a far-off spot of light. Daylight!

He pushed through a small hole and found himself looking out at the great Mississippi rolling by. He ran back for Becky, and they came out together, crying with happiness. They were five miles below the entrance to the cave. Some men in a boat took them home.

That night the church bells rang, and the whole town came out into the streets, shouting, “They're found! They're found!”

Tom and Becky had been lost for three days. About two weeks later Tom went to visit Becky, and Judge Thatcher said, with a smile, “Well, nobody will ever get lost in that cave again. I've had the big door covered with iron and locked.”

Tom turned as white as paper.

“Oh, Judge! Injun Joe's in the cave!”

When the men unlocked the cave door, they found Injun Joe lying dead on the ground. His face was close to the crack under the door, as if he had been trying to see the light outside. His knife lay beside him, broken. He had tried to cut his way through the door, but the iron had beaten him. Tom felt sorry for him in a way. He knew how terrible it was to be lost in the dark.

A few days later Tom took Huck aside. “Huck, the money was never in the town. It's in the cave! That's where I saw Injun Joe.”

They borrowed a small boat and rowed to Tom's secret hole. Deep inside the cave, near the place where Tom had seen Injun Joe, they found a big rock. On it somebody had drawn a cross with candle smoke.

“Number Two, under the cross,” Tom whispered.

They dug under the rock. And there it was: the box, full of gold. The boys filled two small bags and carried them out, almost too excited to breathe.

That evening the Widow Douglas gave a party for the Welshman and his sons, to thank them for saving her life. But Mr. Jones stood up and told everybody the real story: the hero was Huckleberry Finn! The widow was so grateful that she announced she would give Huck a home and send him to school.

“Huck doesn't need it,” said Tom. “Huck's rich!” He ran outside, came back with the two heavy bags and poured the gold out onto the table.

There was over twelve thousand dollars, more than anyone in town had ever seen. It went into the bank, and each boy got a dollar a day from it, as much as the minister earned.

So Huck went to live with the Widow Douglas. She kept him clean and combed, and she taught him to eat with a knife and fork. He had to sleep in clean sheets, go to church and speak politely. After three weeks he disappeared.

Tom found him in an empty barrel, in his old rags, smoking his pipe.

“Tom, being rich ain't as much fun as people think,” Huck said. “The widow's good to me, but I can't stand it. I have to get up at the same time every morning. I can't even scratch! Take my money, Tom. Just give me ten cents now and then.”

Tom thought for a moment. “Huck, I'm starting a gang of robbers. But I can't let you in if you aren't respectable.”

“Can't let me in? But you let me be a pirate!”

“That's different. Robbers are much higher class than pirates. In most countries they're dukes and lords and things like that.”

Huck sighed.

“Well, I'll go back to the widow for a month and try it, if you'll let me be in the gang.”

“It's a deal, Huck! Come along, old friend. And when you're respectable, we'll be the greatest robbers the world has ever seen!”
